title: Impulse and Change in Momentum
short: FΔt = Δp, and the area under a force–time graph is the impulse.
trouble: Students think a ball that bounces back has a smaller change in momentum than one that stops dead.

blocks.html: You know from Newton's second law that a net force changes velocity, and from Softening a Collision that stretching a collision over more time softens it. Impulse puts those two ideas into one equation.

Start from $\Sigma F = ma$ and write the acceleration as $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$. Multiply both sides by $\Delta t$: $$\Sigma F\,\Delta t = m\Delta v = \Delta p.$$ The left side, force times the time it acts, is called the impulse $J$. A big force for a short time and a small force for a long time can give the same impulse, and so the same change in momentum.

Impulse equals change in momentum: $\role[impulse]{momentum}{J} = \role[average force]{force}{F_{\text{avg}}}\role[time interval]{time}{\Delta t} = \role[change in momentum]{momentum}{\Delta p} = \role{mass}{m} \role[final velocity]{velocity}{v_f} - \role{mass}{m} \role[initial velocity]{velocity}{v_i}$. Its unit, $\text{N·s}$, is the same as $\text{kg·m/s}$. When the force changes during the push, the impulse is the area under the force–time graph.

blocks.name: ph-graph

opts.task: Drag the edges of the shaded region. The whole push, from $0$ to $0.4\ \text{s}$, has an area of $6.0\ \text{N·s}$.

blocks.cap: A push that rises, holds and falls. The area under it is the impulse, $6.0\ \text{N·s}$: enough to give a $2.0\ \text{kg}$ cart $3.0\ \text{m/s}$.

blocks.title: Average force from a change in momentum
blocks.q: A $0.43\ \text{kg}$ soccer ball at rest is kicked to $20\ \text{m/s}$. The foot touches it for $0.010\ \text{s}$. What average force acts on the ball?

blocks.title: A bounce versus a stop
blocks.q: A $0.50\ \text{kg}$ ball hits a wall at $6.0\ \text{m/s}$. Find the impulse from the wall (a) if it stops dead and (b) if it bounces straight back at $4.0\ \text{m/s}$. Take "toward the wall" as positive.
steps: (b) After the bounce the velocity is $-4.0\ \text{m/s}$: $$J = (0.50)(-4.0 - 6.0) = -5.0\ \text{N·s}.$$
The bounce needs the bigger impulse: the wall must stop the ball and then throw it back.

blocks.title: Reading the area
blocks.q: A $2.0\ \text{kg}$ cart rolls left at $1.0\ \text{m/s}$. It gets the push in the graph above, to the right. What is its velocity afterward (right positive)?
steps: Area: two triangles, $2 \times \tfrac{1}{2}(0.1)(20) = 2.0\ \text{N·s}$, plus a rectangle, $(0.2)(20) = 4.0\ \text{N·s}$. So $J = 6.0\ \text{N·s}$.

blocks.html: Thinking a bounce changes momentum less than a stop. Speed drops less in a bounce, but momentum is a vector: going from $+6$ to $-4$ is a change of $10$, while going from $+6$ to $0$ is a change of only $6$. Always subtract signed velocities, $v_f - v_i$. Check: a ball that reverses must have an impulse larger than $mv_i$.

blocks.name: ph-collision
blocks.cap: Force against time for a hard and a soft bumper. The areas match (same $\Delta p$), but the soft bumper spreads the impulse over more time, so its peak force is far lower. Switch to "Bounces back" and both areas double.

blocks.html: This is the physics of airbags, gym mats and catching an egg with soft hands: the change in momentum is fixed by the speeds, so the only way to lower the force is to make $\Delta t$ longer. The Momentum and Collisions lab of the Science Lab drops an egg on a pillow and on a floor so you can compare the two force graphs.
